Muscle guarding.text: Reflexive paraspinal splinting is a protective, nociception-driven response to disc, facet, ligament, or muscle irritation without a discrete structural lesion. Its diffuse, non-focal pattern (versus a single strained muscle in L08 or a capsular/extension pattern in L03) supports a non-specific mechanical origin diagnosed by exclusion.

Antalgic posture.text: A pain-avoidance postural deviation that unloads the symptomatic structure. It is a non-specific sign of nociception rather than a lesion-specific marker, consistent with L01's designation as a diagnosis of exclusion once radicular, facet, and red-flag patterns are ruled out.

Lateral shift.text: A trunk lean adopted to offload a painful lumbar segment; per McKenzie's Mechanical Diagnosis and Therapy, a shift without accompanying leg symptoms or neurological signs is treated as a mechanical deformity (not a discogenic radicular sign) and is expected to reduce with repeated-movement testing showing a clear directional preference.
Lateral shift.source: McKenzie, Mechanical Diagnosis and Therapy of the Lumbar Spine

Flattened or increased lordosis.text: Both directions of lordotic change reflect protective adaptation of the lumbar curve: flattening suggests flexion-biased guarding, while increased lordosis suggests extension-biased guarding. The bidirectional (rather than single stereotyped) pattern is itself consistent with L01's non-specific classification, distinct from the single-direction postures seen in L03 (increased lordosis) or L04 (flexed/stooped).

Soft tissue.text: Diffuse paraspinal tenderness and hypertonicity reflect secondary muscular guarding rather than a discrete structural lesion — the expected palpatory pattern in non-specific mechanical LBP, contrasting with the focal tenderness of a facet (L03) or strained muscle (L08).

Segmental.text: Localized segmental tenderness at a single level suggests underlying facet or capsular-ligamentous irritation at that level, useful for guiding manual therapy targeting even when the overall presentation remains non-specific.

Thoracolumbar fascia tightness.text: The thoracolumbar fascia links latissimus dorsi, gluteus maximus, and contralateral trunk musculature into a posterior force-transfer sling; tenderness/tightness here reflects a myofascial contribution to mechanical LBP and often co-occurs with the erector-spinae-dominant, TA-inhibited motor control pattern seen on core assessment.
Thoracolumbar fascia tightness.source: Vleeming et al., self-bracing mechanism of the thoracolumbar fascia and posterior layer

findings: Resisted trunk flexion/extension/side-flexion painless & strong
PA spring test normal/mild stiffness, no single hypermobile or rigid level
sttt.interpretation: Rules out a contractile lesion. Repeated movement assessment (McKenzie-style) is expected to show a directional preference.

cpa.pattern: "Inhibited, erector spinae dominant" is the textbook chronic-LBP CPA finding.

kineticChain.name: Lumbar Segmental Stability Tests
kineticChain.chainEffect: Used as a baseline (prone instability, ASLR, TA drawing-in) — expect normal or only mild TA drawing-in deficit, not a positive prone instability test.

functionalScreen.name: Sit-to-Stand
functionalScreen.note: The general hip-hinge-vs-lumbar-dominant strategy screen; a lumbar-dominant rise pattern here corroborates the TA/erector CPA finding.

L02.name: Lumbar Disc Herniation / Radiculopathy
recommended: Femoral nerve tension test (if upper lumbar)

Antalgic lean.text: Trunk shift away from or toward the symptomatic side changes the position of the disc relative to the adjacent nerve root: a lean away from the painful side typically indicates the herniation lies lateral to the root (shifting away reduces compression), while a lean toward the side suggests a medial (axillary) herniation — the direction helps localize the disc-root relationship.
Antalgic lean.source: McKenzie, Mechanical Diagnosis and Therapy of the Lumbar Spine; Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment, Ch.9

Dermatomal signs.text: Sensory changes confined to a specific dermatome map directly to the level of nerve root compression, distinguishing this radicular (single-root) presentation from the non-specific, non-dermatomal referred pain of L01.

Possible foot-drop.text: Weakness of ankle/great-toe dorsiflexion (tibialis anterior, EHL) indicates motor compromise of the L4 or L5 nerve root from disc compression. A significant or rapidly progressing foot drop is itself a relative red flag that should prompt urgent escalation and cross-check against the L11 red-flag screen.

Lateral shift / flattened lordosis.text: An antalgic lateral shift, often with loss of lordosis, is a classic disc-herniation postural sign; McKenzie's system describes it as a deformity that may or may not centralize with lateral correction. Unlike the similar-looking shift in L01, here it typically co-presents with dermatomal leg symptoms and a positive SLR/Slump.
Lateral shift / flattened lordosis.source: McKenzie, Mechanical Diagnosis and Therapy of the Lumbar Spine

Neural (sciatic) lower-limb tension line.text: Tenderness or symptom reproduction along the course of the sciatic nerve (piriformis, popliteal fossa, peroneal tunnel) reflects mechanosensitivity of neural tissue secondary to root compression/inflammation, correlating with a positive SLR or Slump test rather than a capsular or muscular source.
Neural (sciatic) lower-limb tension line.source: Butler, Mobilisation of the Nervous System; Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment, Ch.9

specialTests: Femoral nerve tension test (if upper lumbar)

findings: Resisted hip/knee myotome tests (L4 quads, L5 EHL, S1 calf) may be weak & painless
Passive SLR/Slump reproduces leg pain
sttt.interpretation: Root involvement (not a contractile lesion) is supported — myotome weakness is painless (root pattern), and passive SLR/Slump reproduces neural, not capsular, pain.

muscles.name: Multifidus (at the herniated level)
muscles.state: Secondarily inhibited — recheck once acute phase settles

cpa.pattern: Not a classic muscle-pair pattern (neural compression). Recheck Multifidus at the herniated level once the acute phase settles — often secondarily inhibited.

kineticChain.name: Lumbar Flexion Control (Waiter's Bow)

fields.label: Forward bending pattern
options: Lateral trunk shift reducing on return

kineticChain.chainEffect: Watch for the "aberrant movement, painful arc" pattern — a lateral trunk shift on forward bending that reduces on return is explicitly documented as indicating disc herniation.

functionalScreen.name: Forward Bend (lateral shift + centralisation screen)
functionalScreen.note: The direct McKenzie-style functional correlate of this condition.

Extension-aggravated posture.text: Patients position the trunk to avoid extension because it approximates and compresses the zygapophyseal joint surfaces on the symptomatic side while narrowing the intervertebral foramen — the same mechanism that produces a positive Kemp's/Quadrant test.

Unilateral muscle guarding.text: One-sided paraspinal spasm reflects capsular irritation of a single zygapophyseal joint, a more focal pattern than the bilateral/diffuse guarding typical of L01.

Increased lordosis.text: Excessive lumbar extension increases facet joint compressive loading and narrows the space between adjacent articular surfaces, a recognized driver of facet-mediated pain.

Rotation restriction.text: Limited rotation toward the involved side reflects a capsular restriction pattern at the symptomatic facet joint, consistent with the joint-play findings expected on Passive Physiological Intervertebral Movement testing at that level.
Rotation restriction.source: Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment, Ch.9 (Cyriax capsular pattern concept)

Lumbar paraspinal fascial tightness.text: Secondary myofascial guarding overlying the irritated facet joint; this diffuse fascial finding should be differentiated from the discrete segmental hypomobility/tenderness found on PA spring testing directly over the joint at that level.

passive.label: PA spring test at the level

findings: Resisted trunk movements painless
Passive extension + rotation (Kemp's) reproduces local pain with a capsular end-feel
PA spring hypomobile/painful at the level
sttt.interpretation: Rules out a contractile lesion; capsular-pattern findings on passive extension/rotation localize the source to the facet joint.

cpa.pattern: "Inhibited, unilateral" classically co-occurs with segmental facet irritation.

kineticChain.name: Lumbar Rotation Control
kineticChain.chainEffect: A stiff thoracic spine forcing lumbar load-bearing rotation can drive facet loading — check thoracic rotation before treating the facet in isolation.

functionalScreen.name: Squat Pattern
functionalScreen.note: Watch the return-to-stand (extension) phase specifically, since facet loading is most provoked there.

Flexed posture.text: Patients adopt lumbar flexion because it enlarges the central canal and neural foraminal cross-sectional area and reduces ligamentum flavum buckling, decompressing cauda equina/nerve roots and relieving neurogenic claudication — the classic stooped ('simian') stenosis posture.
Flexed posture.source: Katz & Harris, "Clinical Practice: Lumbar Spinal Stenosis," NEJM 2008; Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment, Ch.9

Wide-based gait.text: A broader base of support compensates for proprioceptive deficit and mild lower-limb weakness from chronic nerve root/cauda equina compromise, and also reduces spinal extension during ambulation, both improving stability and symptom tolerance.

Stooped forward posture relieving sympto.text: Flexion increases canal and foraminal cross-sectional area, directly explaining why forward-flexed postures — classically, leaning on a shopping cart — relieve neurogenic claudication; this is the inverse of the extension-relief pattern seen in facet dysfunction (L03).
Stooped forward posture relieving sympto.source: Katz & Harris, "Clinical Practice: Lumbar Spinal Stenosis," NEJM 2008

Neural canal / foraminal narrowing patte.text: Reduced space for neural elements, as documented on imaging, correlates with reproducible leg symptoms on passive extension and relief on flexion — the physiological basis for using the extension/flexion provocation pattern (and the Bicycle Test of van Gelderen) to differentiate stenosis from a disc-herniation pattern.
Neural canal / foraminal narrowing patte.source: Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment, Ch.9; "Bicycle test" of van Gelderen, J Neurosurg 1977

findings: Resisted tests generally painless (non-contractile)
Passive extension reproduces leg symptoms (canal narrows)
Flexion relieves — the inverse of a typical disc pattern
sttt.interpretation: Bicycle test / stoop test and treadmill testing (neurogenic vs vascular claudication) are the key provocative maneuvers for distinguishing stenosis from a disc pattern.

muscles.name: TA / Multifidus
muscles.state: Often globally inhibited from long-standing guarding

muscles.name: Glute Max
muscles.state: Frequently also inhibited from reduced walking tolerance (deconditioning)

cpa.pattern: Global inhibition pattern from long-standing guarding and deconditioning.

kineticChain.name: Lumbar Flexion Control
kineticChain.chainEffect: Expect the inverse of the disc pattern: flexion-biased postures relieve, extension provokes; a McKenzie flexion preference here fits stenosis rather than herniation.

functionalScreen.name: Squat Pattern
functionalScreen.note: Assess tolerance for a flexion-biased loading strategy, since gait-based bicycle/stoop provocation (STTT above) isn't part of this app's seated/standing functional screen set.

L05.name: Sacroiliac Joint (SIJ) Dysfunction
required: SIJ provocation CLUSTER: Compression, Distraction, Sacral Thrust, Gaenslen's, FABERE/Patrick, Gillet's
recommended: Palpation (PSIS, sacral sulcus — weak inter-rater reliability)
ESR/CRP/HLA-B27 referral if inflammatory features co-exist

Pelvic asymmetry.text: Visual asymmetry of iliac crest or ASIS height has historically been used to infer SIJ malposition, but static bony-landmark observation for asymmetry has demonstrated poor inter-rater reliability and does not correlate well with symptomatic SIJ pain; modern SIJ diagnosis instead relies on the pain-provocation test cluster.
Pelvic asymmetry.source: Laslett, "Evidence-Based Diagnosis and Treatment of the Painful Sacroiliac Joint," J Man Manip Ther 2008

PSIS level difference.text: PSIS height differences are common in asymptomatic individuals and do not reliably localize SIJ dysfunction on their own; this finding should be interpreted only alongside a positive provocation cluster, not as an independent diagnostic marker.
PSIS level difference.source: Laslett, "Evidence-Based Diagnosis and Treatment of the Painful Sacroiliac Joint," J Man Manip Ther 2008

Innominate rotation / leg-length discrep.text: Apparent leg-length asymmetry or an anteriorly/posteriorly rotated innominate is a proposed but poorly validated static marker of SIJ dysfunction. Like the observation findings above, isolated static 'malalignment' findings correlate weakly with symptomatic SIJ pain and should not substitute for dynamic pain-provocation testing.
Innominate rotation / leg-length discrep.source: Physio-pedia, Sacroiliac Joint Special Test Cluster; Laslett 2008

PSIS.text: Point tenderness over the PSIS is a commonly used but weakly reliable localizing sign for SIJ dysfunction and is retained here only as a supportive, not primary, finding.
PSIS.source: Laslett, "Evidence-Based Diagnosis and Treatment of the Painful Sacroiliac Joint," J Man Manip Ther 2008

Sacral sulcus — weak inter-rater reliabi.text: Tenderness or apparent deepening of the sacral sulcus has been proposed to reflect sacral torsion but demonstrates poor inter-examiner agreement in validity studies. Note: the condition library's own required-test list names six sub-tests under the SIJ provocation cluster (Compression, Distraction, Sacral Thrust, Gaenslen's, FABERE/Patrick, Gillet's) while its scoring rule states '3+ of 5 positive.' Researching Laslett's original validated cluster (Laslett et al. 2005, J Manipulative Physiol Ther) resolves the arithmetic but not the naming: the validated pain-provocation cluster used for the '3+ of 5' rule comprises five true provocation tests — Distraction, Compression, Thigh Thrust (posterior shear), Sacral Thrust, and Gaenslen's — with 3-of-5 positive giving ~91% sensitivity/78% specificity for SIJ pain. Gillet's test is a motion-palpation (mobility) test, not a pain-provocation test, and standing/sitting flexion and Gillet's have separately been shown to have poor inter-rater reliability (van der Wurff et al. 2000), which is likely why it and FABER/Patrick are inconsistently bundled into the 'six named tests' description versus excluded from the validated five-test scored cluster. This discrepancy is flagged rather than silently resolved, per the source library's own caveat.
Sacral sulcus — weak inter-rater reliabi.source: Laslett et al., "Diagnosis of Sacroiliac Joint Pain: Validity of Individual Provocation Tests and Composites of Tests," Man Ther 2005; van der Wurff et al., reliability of SIJ tests, 2000

Posterior sacroiliac ligament / thoracol.text: Tenderness over the long dorsal sacroiliac ligament and thoracolumbar fascia reflects the posterior myofascial 'force closure' sling (gluteus maximus, biceps femoris, thoracolumbar fascia, contralateral latissimus dorsi) implicated in SIJ load transfer; this often accompanies the glute-max-inhibited, QL-dominant pattern found on core/motor-control assessment.
Posterior sacroiliac ligament / thoracol.source: Vleeming et al., self-bracing mechanism of the sacroiliac joint

findings: Resisted hip abduction/extension may be painful secondarily (glute med/involved musculature)
The SIJ provocation cluster is the primary joint-play equivalent
sttt.interpretation: SIJ provocation cluster: 3+ of 5 positive = SIJ source; active SLR is also part of the required battery. (Note: the source lists six named sub-tests under "cluster" — Compression, Distraction, Sacral Thrust, Gaenslen's, FABERE/Patrick, Gillet's — while its own scoring rule refers to "3+ of 5"; both are reproduced verbatim here.)

cpa.pattern: "Inhibited, QL dominant" is the classic driver of SIJ-pattern pain via altered force closure.

kineticChain.name: Lumbar Segmental Stability's Active Straight Leg Raise component
kineticChain.chainEffect: Manual ASIS compression improving the ASLR is the direct documented sign of an SIJ force-closure deficit.

functionalScreen.name: Single Leg Stance (SIJ & Lumbopelvic Control / Trendelenburg)
functionalScreen.note: The named functional test for exactly this pattern.

L06.name: Lumbar Instability
required: Observation for instability jog during active movement
observation: Instability jog / catch during active movement
posture: Excessive segmental motion on PA spring

Instability jog / catch during active mo.text: A visible 'catch,' jerky deviation, or momentary give-way during active trunk flexion/extension reflects a segment moving beyond neuromuscular control at the extremes of its neutral zone. Per Panjabi's spinal stability model, this represents failure of the active (muscular) and neural (control) subsystems to compensate for excess laxity in the passive (ligamentous/disc) subsystem.
Instability jog / catch during active mo.source: Panjabi, "The Stabilizing System of the Spine, Parts I & II," J Spinal Disord 1992

Excessive segmental motion on PA spring.text: Hypermobility detected on passive PA glide at a single level indicates an enlarged neutral zone at that segment — Panjabi identified an enlarged neutral zone, not gross range of motion, as the direct clinical correlate of spinal instability.
Excessive segmental motion on PA spring.source: Panjabi, "The Stabilizing System of the Spine, Part II: Neutral Zone and Instability Hypothesis," J Spinal Disord 1992

Deep segmental stabiliser insufficiency.text: Reduced or absent recruitment of multifidus/transversus abdominis under light load indicates active-subsystem failure to control the neutral zone — consistent with Panjabi's model in which instability arises from inadequate muscular compensation for passive-system laxity rather than gross structural failure alone.
Deep segmental stabiliser insufficiency.source: Panjabi, "The Stabilizing System of the Spine, Part I," J Spinal Disord 1992; Hodges & Richardson, transversus abdominis/multifidus motor control studies

findings: Resisted trunk tests may be strong but poorly controlled (an instability "catch" on active movement, not true weakness)
Passive PA spring shows a hypermobile segment
sttt.interpretation: Prone instability test and H & I stability tests are the primary provocative maneuvers for this condition.

cpa.pattern: "Inhibited, bilateral" with erector-spinae global substitution is the textbook instability CPA pattern.

kineticChain.name: Lumbar Segmental Stability Tests

fields.label: Prone instability test / ASLR / abdominal drawing-in

kineticChain.chainEffect: The direct match: prone instability test, ASLR, and abdominal drawing-in are this app's own instability battery.

functionalScreen.name: Rotary Stability (FMS) + Trunk Stability Push-Up (FMS)
functionalScreen.note: The two generic core-stability screens most directly relevant to a diagnosed instability.

L07.name: Spondylolisthesis / Spondylolysis
recommended: SPECT/MRI if x-ray negative but suspicion high
Meyerding grading once imaging confirms slip

Palpable step deformity.text: A palpable 'step-off' between adjacent spinous processes reflects anterior translation of one vertebral body relative to the one below via bilateral pars interarticularis defects. Combined with a positive Stork test, this is one of the few observation findings specific enough to warrant imaging confirmation and subsequent Meyerding grading (percentage of anterior translation: Grade I 0–25%, II 25–50%, III 50–75%, IV 75–100%, V >100%/spondyloptosis).
Palpable step deformity.source: Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment, Ch.9; Meyerding grading classification

Hamstring tightness.text: Reflexive hamstring guarding is a well-documented compensatory finding in spondylolisthesis, thought to reduce anterior pelvic tilt and lumbar lordosis to protect the unstable segment, and is disproportionate to any true hamstring muscle shortness.

Increased lordosis at slip level.text: Anterior vertebral translation shifts the center of gravity forward, provoking a compensatory increase in lordosis at and around the slip level to keep posture upright — this paradoxically increases shear loading through the pars interarticularis and can perpetuate progression of the slip.

Pars interarticularis / anterior longitu.text: Localized tenderness over the pars interarticularis reflects the site of the bony defect (spondylolysis) or an active stress reaction; anterior longitudinal ligament tension/tenderness reflects chronic stretch from sustained anterior vertebral translation.

resisted.label: Resisted trunk extension
options: Reproduces pain at the pars/slip level

findings: Resisted trunk extension reproduces pain at the pars/slip level (the Stork test is this same single-leg extension provocation)
Passive extension is often the most provocative movement
sttt.interpretation: Stork test (single-leg hyperextension) reproducing pain is the key provocative finding for this condition.

muscles.name: TA + Multifidus (segmental stabilisers, at the slip level)
muscles.state: Assess as for Lumbar Instability's core-stability logic

cpa.pattern: Same core-stability logic as Lumbar Instability (L06), since dynamic segmental control limits further slip.

kineticChain.name: Lumbar Segmental Stability Tests + Lumbar Flexion Control

fields.label: Prone instability test at the slip level

kineticChain.chainEffect: The prone instability test at the slip level, plus watching for extension-provoked pain (the stork-test principle applied functionally).

functionalScreen.name: Sit-to-Stand / Squat Pattern
functionalScreen.note: Note any pain specifically on the extension/return phase, mirroring the Stork test's single-leg hyperextension provocation.

L08.name: Lumbar Muscle Strain
recommended: X-ray only if red flags present
observation: Visible muscle spasm / guarding on movement
posture: Antalgic lean away from strained side

Visible muscle spasm / guarding on movem.text: Acute reflexive contraction of the injured muscle (commonly erector spinae or quadratus lumborum) limits further stretch of torn fibers — a direct contractile-tissue protective response. Its localization to one identifiable muscle, correlating with a strong-and-painful resisted test, distinguishes it from L01's more diffuse guarding.
Visible muscle spasm / guarding on movem.source: Cyriax, Textbook of Orthopaedic Medicine (selective tension / contractile lesion pattern)

Antalgic lean away from strained side.text: Trunk lean away from the involved side shortens and unloads the strained muscle belly, minimizing tensile stress at the site of the tear during static posture.

Localize strained muscle.text: Point tenderness at the muscle belly or musculotendinous junction localizes the acute strain, consistent with Cyriax's selective-tension principle that pairs a palpation finding with a strong-and-painful resisted test in that muscle's specific line of action.

Paraspinal / quadratus lumborum fascial.text: Secondary fascial tightening around the strained muscle reflects compensatory guarding of the surrounding myofascial sling; per the condition's own motor-control note, this should be differentiated from the primary strain site to check whether QL/erector spinae is the true lesion or an overactive compensator (e.g., secondary to TA/glute max inhibition).

resisted.label: Resisted trunk movement in the direction of strain

passive.label: Passive stretch of the same muscle

findings: Resisted trunk movement in the direction of strain is strong but painful (classic Cyriax contractile-lesion pattern)
Passive stretch of the same muscle is also painful
sttt.interpretation: Resisted isometric movements reproduce pain — per Cyriax classification, strong + painful = contractile lesion.

muscles.name: Erector Spinae or QL (whichever strained)
muscles.state: Check whether primary strain or an overactive compensator (2° to TA/glute max inhibition)

cpa.pattern: Check whether it's a primary strain or an OVERACTIVE COMPENSATOR before treating as isolated.

kineticChain.name: Lumbar Flexion Control
kineticChain.chainEffect: Expect a guarded, direction-specific restriction (pain-limited, not a true motor-control fault); reassess as the strain settles.

functionalScreen.name: Sit-to-Stand
functionalScreen.note: Document the guarded rise strategy at baseline to track recovery of a normal hip-hinge pattern.

L09.name: Lumbar Myofascial Pain
required: Palpation for taut bands/trigger points reproducing referred pain
palpation: Taut bands/trigger points reproducing referred pain
Myofascial trigger point / taut band network

Taut bands.text: A palpable taut band is the defining physical sign of a myofascial trigger point — a localized region of sustained sarcomere contracture within the muscle — per Travell & Simons' integrated trigger point hypothesis, the same mechanism underlying the cervical myofascial presentation (cross-reference C10).
Taut bands.source: Travell & Simons, Myofascial Pain and Dysfunction: The Trigger Point Manual

Trigger points on palpation.text: Direct palpation reproducing the patient's familiar referred pain pattern — not just local tenderness — is the clinical criterion that distinguishes an active trigger point from simple soft-tissue tenderness, and is the key diagnostic finding required for this condition.
Trigger points on palpation.source: Travell & Simons, Myofascial Pain and Dysfunction: The Trigger Point Manual

Sustained-posture loading pattern.text: Prolonged static postural loading (e.g., sustained lumbar flexion at a desk or during repetitive lifting) is the classic perpetuating factor for trigger point development, via sustained low-level motor unit activity and localized muscle ischemia in the QL/erector spinae group.
Sustained-posture loading pattern.source: Travell & Simons, Myofascial Pain and Dysfunction: The Trigger Point Manual

Taut bands/trigger points reproducing re.text: Reproduction of referred (not just local) pain on palpation is the clinical criterion that establishes the palpated point as the actual symptom generator, differentiating myofascial referral from a structural joint source such as the facet (L03) or SIJ (L05).
Taut bands/trigger points reproducing re.source: Travell & Simons, Myofascial Pain and Dysfunction: The Trigger Point Manual

Myofascial trigger point / taut band net.text: QL and erector spinae trigger points classically refer pain to the buttock, groin, and lower lumbar/SI region — patterns that can mimic SIJ or facet pain and should be distinguished from those structural sources using the palpation reproduction criterion above, consistent with this condition's own note that it is often the symptom of a deeper glute-inhibition pattern rather than a primary muscle problem.
Myofascial trigger point / taut band net.source: Travell & Simons, Myofascial Pain and Dysfunction: The Trigger Point Manual

resisted.label: Resisted test of muscle under trigger-point suspicion
options: Reproduces referred (not true) pain, no true weakness

findings: Resisted tests reproduce referred (not true) pain from the palpated trigger point, no true weakness
sttt.interpretation: Palpation reproducing the referred pain pattern is the key finding for this condition.

cpa.pattern: This is very often the SYMPTOM of a deeper glute-inhibition pattern, not a primary muscle problem.

kineticChain.reason: Not primarily a joint-mobility condition (myofascial referral) — the Single Leg Stance / hip-focused screens are more informative than a lumbar mobility test.

functionalScreen.name: Sit-to-Stand / Forward Bend
functionalScreen.note: Check whether a lumbar-flexion-dominant strategy is loading these exact muscles, consistent with the CPA finding above.

L10.name: Inflammatory Back Pain (Axial Spondyloarthritis Pattern)
required: Lumbar AROM all planes (uniform vs single-plane restriction)

Global restriction.text: Lumbar AROM restricted symmetrically and uniformly across all planes — rather than a single-plane/capsular pattern — reflects a systemic inflammatory process affecting the sacroiliac joints, spinal entheses, and facet capsules diffusely, rather than a discrete mechanical lesion. This non-capsular, global pattern is the key functional finding distinguishing axial spondyloarthritis from the directional-preference conditions L01–L09.
Global restriction.source: ASAS classification criteria for axial spondyloarthritis; Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment, Ch.9

Morning stiffness posture.text: Prolonged morning stiffness (classically >30–60 minutes, improving with activity/NSAIDs and worsening with rest) is a core feature of inflammatory back pain per the Calin criteria incorporated into the ASAS classification approach, reflecting inflammation-driven pain physiology rather than the rest-relieved, activity-aggravated pattern typical of mechanical LBP.
Morning stiffness posture.source: Calin et al., inflammatory back pain criteria; ASAS classification criteria for axial spondyloarthritis

Flattened lumbar lordosis.text: Progressive loss of lumbar lordosis reflects paraspinal muscle spasm early in disease and, in established disease, structural involvement (enthesitis, syndesmophyte formation, eventual ankylosis) of the anterior and posterior spinal ligamentous structures and facet joints — an early postural marker that should prompt screening for axial spondyloarthritis.
Flattened lumbar lordosis.source: Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment, Ch.9; ASAS classification criteria for axial spondyloarthritis

Reduced chest expansion.text: Reduced chest expansion (classically <2.5 cm) reflects costovertebral and costosternal joint involvement by the same systemic inflammatory process — a classic extraspinal sign incorporated into the modified New York criteria for ankylosing spondylitis and correlated with disease chronicity.
Reduced chest expansion.source: Modified New York criteria for Ankylosing Spondylitis

specialTests: FABER Test (+ posterior SIJ provocation — cross-refer L05)

findings: Resisted tests generally painless early (inflammatory, not mechanical)
Passive ROM uniformly restricted, non-capsular
sttt.interpretation: AROM uniformly restricted in all planes (non-capsular pattern) is the defining functional finding for this condition.

cpa.reason: Not applicable — systemic inflammatory diagnosis, not a motor-control compensation pattern.

kineticChain.name: Lumbar Flexion Control + Rotation Control
kineticChain.chainEffect: Expect GLOBAL, non-directional restriction rather than the directional preference seen in L01–L09.

functionalScreen.name: Sit-to-Stand + Forward Bend
functionalScreen.note: Both should show symmetric, globally reduced range rather than a specific direction of preference.

L11.name: Serious Pathology / Red Flag
L11.body: Cauda equina indicator → EMERGENCY same-day referral. Fracture, inflammatory, or other serious-pathology red flag → URGENT referral before continuing.
L11.action: Replaces the differential list entirely when triggered. No module cards or test suggestions render. STTT/CPA: not applicable — do not resisted-test or compensation-test until the red flag is cleared.
